newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - FINNISH MARKETS START COMFY WITH ERM LINK.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - FINNISH MARKETS START COMFY WITH ERM LINK.

text.p: The Finnish markka was comfortably steady and bonds firmed but forestry stocks eased in edgy Monday trade after the markka was linked to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) at the weekend.
The link came at a more or less expected central parity rate -- 3.04 per German mark -- and analysts said this would not bring any pressure on Finnish exporters' competitiveness.
"From the point of view of fundamentals and competitiveness, this level was quite OK," said Postipankki chief economist Ari Aaltonen.
He said the central parity rate felt comfortable but warned that the stable intitial reaction could partly be caused by the fact that operators were not yet used to the new regime.

At 1320/1020 GMT, the markka stood at 2.9875 compared to 2.9860 at Friday's close after trading in a tight 2.9860-2.9880 range. An overnight weakening in Singapore came in very thin volume and dealers said it was meaningless.
With the markka now tied to the central parity rate with 15 percent fluctuation bands either way, dealers expected a narrower notional band although the central bank denied this.
"It looks as though the situation resembles that of 1993 when we moved to a floating regime, markets are not quite used to this yet," said Aaltonen.
Finnish central bank governor Sirkka Hamalainen said she was pleased with the markets' reaction so far to the move, and that the markka's level was fully driven by the market.
"That's why we have been very pleased with the exchange rate level and stablility (today) because it is fully market driven," she said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
In ERM, international foreign exchange trends and expectations of EMU progress become much more important to drive the market than Finnish fundamentals.
Bond yields fell and there was scope for further gains as Finland was expected to continue converging with Germany as long as EMU looks like staying on track, dealers said.
"We expect the (2006) gap over Germany to fall to 25 basis points ... in a month or so," said Henrik Alsoe, economist at Danish Unibank.
However, he added this was based on a bullish scenario for German and U.S. bond markets -- a more stable international trend would make convergence much slower.
Stocks were mixed with forestries under slight pressure amid some concern the Finnish industry may lose competitive ground if the Swedish crown weakens in relation to the now pegged markka.
The HEX index was off a marginal 0.04 percent at 2,183.93, bolstered by Merita Bank while the forestries' sub-index lost 1.1 percent.
UPM-Kymmene fell three percent at its first trade but recovered to slightly weaker levels. It stood at 93.30 markka, down 1.20, in the early afternoon.
"Some investors seem to be uncertain about effects of this link, but I think it will be beneficial for Finnish stocks in the longer term as it lowers the country risk," one broker said.
